blocks.text: Given a staircase with n steps, and the ability to climb either 1 or 2 steps at a time, count how many distinct ways there are to reach the top.

blocks.title: Analogy: Every Path Ends With One Final Move
blocks.text: Whatever path is taken to reach the top of the staircase, the very last move taken must have been either a single step or a double step. That means the number of ways to reach step n is exactly the number of ways to reach step n minus 1, plus the number of ways to reach step n minus 2, since those are the only two places the final move could have started from.

blocks.caption: The last move is either a single step or a double step

blocks.text: There are 2 distinct ways to reach the second step.
There are 3 distinct ways to reach the third step.
Only a single move is possible, one step, so there is exactly 1 way.
Before writing any code, it is worth checking whether this counting problem matches a recurrence already solved elsewhere in the sheet.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Whatever path reaches step n, its very last move was either a single step, arriving from step n minus 1, or a double step, arriving from step n minus 2, and those two cases can never overlap.

Observation 2: That means the count for step n is exactly the count for step n minus 1 plus the count for step n minus 2, which is precisely the Fibonacci recurrence, just shifted by one position and with different starting values.

Observation 3: Testing small cases confirms it, 1 way for step 1, 2 ways for step 2, 3 ways for step 3, 5 ways for step 4, the same growth pattern as the Fibonacci sequence.

Observation 4: Since the Fibonacci Number problem in Coding Foundations already worked through exactly this progression, naive recursion, then a stored array, then two rolling variables, the same three techniques apply here directly, with no new derivation needed.
Naming this as Fibonacci in disguise turns what looks like a brand new counting problem into a direct application of a recurrence already fully understood.

For any step n, the last move must have been a single step from step n minus 1, or a double step from step n minus 2. Recursively count the ways to reach each of those two earlier steps, and add the results together.

items: If n is 1 or 2, return n directly, these are the base cases.
Otherwise, recursively find the number of ways to reach step n minus 1.
Recursively find the number of ways to reach step n minus 2.
Add the two results together and return that sum.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: recursively try a final 1 step move and a final 2 step move, then add the results

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The base cases return n directly rather than a fixed constant, since conveniently, the count for step 1 and step 2 both happen to equal n itself, 1 and 2 respectively.
Both recursive calls are made unconditionally, since the last move genuinely could have been either a single or a double step, there is no way to rule either one out ahead of time.
The two recursive results are simply added, mirroring the reasoning directly, the total ways to reach step n is the ways from each of the two possible prior positions combined.

blocks.text: This is correct, since every possible path to step n is accounted for exactly once, split by what its final move must have been.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(2 to the power n), the same exponential recursion tree shape as naive Fibonacci, since climbStairs(n minus 2) gets recomputed independently many times over.
Space: O(n), for the depth of the recursion call stack.

Limitation: the recursion recomputes the exact same smaller step counts an enormous number of times. Since the number of ways to reach any given step only ever needs to be computed once, storing each result the first time it is computed avoids all of that repeated work.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why the recursion works but is wasteful: the exact same smaller step counts, especially the ones closest to n, get recomputed independently an enormous number of times, exactly the naive Fibonacci problem.

What stays the same as Fibonacci: the underlying recurrence itself, each value depends only on the two values immediately before it.

What removes the repeated work: computing each step count exactly once, from the bottom up, starting at the two known base cases and storing every result as it is produced.

Can the same stored-array technique from Fibonacci be reused unchanged: yes, an array indexed by step number, filled from step 1 up to step n, applies here with no modification beyond the different base case values.

The core idea: build the ways array from the bottom up, computing ways[i] as ways[i minus 1] plus ways[i minus 2], reusing every previously computed value instead of recomputing it.

Build the answer from the bottom up instead of top down. Store the number of ways to reach every step from 1 up to n in an array, starting from the two known base cases, and computing each later step directly from the two values already stored just before it.
Build an array of step counts from the bottom up, starting at the two known base cases and combining the two previous values at every later step.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: build up the ways array from the base cases, one step at a time

blocks.text: This works because ways[i] is defined as exactly ways[i minus 1] plus ways[i minus 2], the same recurrence used in the brute force, but each value is now computed only once, in order from step 1 up to step n, so every value it depends on is already available and correct by the time it is needed.

items: ways[1] and ways[2] are set directly to the known base case values before the main loop begins.
The loop starts at i equal to 3, since the first two values are already filled in, and proceeds upward through n.
Each ways[i] is computed as the sum of the two immediately preceding, already-finalized entries, exactly mirroring the recursive definition but without ever repeating work.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a genuine complexity class improvement, every step is computed exactly once.
Space: O(n), for the array holding every step's result.

Computing the number of ways to reach step i only ever needs the two most recently computed values, everything further back is never looked at again. Instead of storing an entire array, just two variables are enough, updated and slid forward on every iteration.

blocks.caption: Further optimization: keep only the two most recent values and slide them forward

items: prev2 and prev1 are initialized to the two base case values, exactly replacing what ways[1] and ways[2] held in the array version.
Each iteration computes current as the sum of the two rolling variables, the same recurrence as before, just without an array to index into.
Both variables slide forward by one position at the end of each iteration, prev2 takes prev1's old value and prev1 takes the newly computed current, discarding anything older than that.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), the same as the array based version.
Space: O(1) extra space, the real floor for this problem, since only the two most recently computed values are ever needed at once.

blocks.text: This problem is the Fibonacci sequence in disguise, the number of ways to climb n stairs is exactly the (n plus 1)th Fibonacci number, and the same progression, naive recursion, then a stored array, then two rolling variables, applies here just as it did there.

items: Using plain recursion without any memoization, which recomputes the same step counts an exponential number of times.
Getting the base cases wrong, there is exactly 1 way to reach step 1 and exactly 2 ways to reach step 2.
Forgetting that only the two most recent values are ever needed, and storing an entire array when it is not necessary.

blocks.text: Explicitly naming this as the same recurrence as Fibonacci, and explaining why, the last move splits every path into exactly two cases, is a fast way to justify jumping straight to the dynamic programming solution without deriving it from scratch.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "does this remind you of anything", think: this is exactly the Fibonacci recurrence, just with different base case values.
If the interviewer says "can you avoid the exponential recursion", think: build the answer bottom up in an array, or reduce further to two rolling variables.
If the interviewer says "can you do this in constant space", think: only the two most recent values are ever needed, keep just those.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force recursion runs in O(2 to the power n) time and O(n) space for the call stack. The array based dynamic programming approach runs in O(n) time and O(n) space, a genuine complexity class improvement. The rolling two variable version keeps the same O(n) time while reducing space to O(1), the real floor for this problem.

items: Pattern: dynamic programming through a recurrence built by splitting on the last decision, structurally identical to the Fibonacci recurrence already solved in the Coding Foundations category.
Core Idea: the number of ways to reach step n is exactly the ways to reach step n minus 1 plus the ways to reach step n minus 2, since the very last move is always either a single or a double step.
Time: O(2 to the power n) for the brute force, O(n) for both the array based and rolling variable optimized versions.
Space: O(n) call stack depth for the brute force, O(n) for the array version, O(1) extra for the rolling variable version.
Most Important Observation: a new counting problem is often an already-solved recurrence wearing a different costume, here Fibonacci with different base cases.
Interview Difficulty: easy to write the brute force recursion; recognizing the Fibonacci connection immediately is what shows real pattern recognition.
One line memory trick: ways[i] equals ways[i minus 1] plus ways[i minus 2], Fibonacci with base cases 1 and 2.
